issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact are not disturbed in a special-leave appeal absent a substantial legal or procedural defect or grave injustice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found that the plaintiffs had not proved title to the disputed property and dismissed their claim for possession.
The plaintiffs challenged the concurrent findings in a special-leave appeal, relying on the interpretation of title documents and the defendants’ alleged adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were not displaced; they could not be disturbed without a qualifying error or injustice, although construction of a title document raises a question of law and whether possession is adverse is partly a question of fact and partly a question of law.
issues.legal_principle: In a special-leave appeal, concurrent findings of fact are not disturbed merely because another view is possible. Intervention may be justified by such matters as miscarriage of justice, procedural or legal error, material evidence being overlooked, perversity, or grave injustice. A substantial question of law is required. The Court followed Kaolapati v. Amar, Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. The Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Jadu Gopal v. Panna Lal, and Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. The Commissioner of Income-tax; Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Benahi Khare was distinguished.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brought an appeal by special leave from the lower courts’ decision.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same findings of fact.
predicates.no_exceptional_error_shown: The challenging party did not establish a qualifying legal, procedural, evidentiary, or justice-related defect in those findings.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges concurrent factual findings and no exceptional defect is established, those findings remain undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: Construction of a title document depends on the parties’ manifested intention, including their acts and the property actually delivered pursuant to the transaction.
material_facts: The plaintiffs relied on sale deeds and a court decree as the source of their predecessor’s title to the disputed land.
The deeds referred to a larger survey number, but the partition decree and commissioner’s plan did not include the disputed portion.
The property delivered pursuant to the decree was treated as the property the parties had demarcated and accepted.
issues.conclusion: The deeds and decree, construed in light of the parties’ intention and their acts, did not establish that the plaintiffs’ predecessor acquired title to the disputed land.
issues.legal_principle: Construction of a document of title is a question of law. The parties’ intention may be gathered from the words used and from their acts; delivery gives effect to a deed, and what was delivered pursuant to a decree may clarify the property covered by it. Under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, delivery of tangible property occurs when the seller places the buyer, or a person directed by the buyer, in possession. Section 55(1) requires the seller, on being required, to give such possession as the nature of the property permits.

rule.if: title_claim_proceeding and title_instruments_claim_land and (instrument_scope_excludes_land or delivery_excludes_land)

predicates.title_claim_proceeding: A claimant sought recognition of title to land in a court proceeding.
predicates.title_instruments_claim_land: The claimant relied on documents or a decree said to convey or allot the land.
predicates.instrument_scope_excludes_land: The words and context of the relied-on documents, construed in light of the parties’ manifested intention, did not include the claimed land.
predicates.delivery_excludes_land: The land delivered or allotted pursuant to the transaction or decree did not include the claimed land.

issues.definition: A title claim based on documents or a decree fails as to land excluded by the instruments’ scope or by the property actually delivered.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of adverse possession against a claimant does not arise when that claimant has not established title to the land.
material_facts: The defendants asserted that they or their predecessors had possessed parts of the property for many years and had acquired title by adverse possession.
The Court found that the plaintiffs had not proved that their predecessor acquired title to the disputed land.
The Court therefore held that adverse possession against the plaintiffs did not arise.
issues.conclusion: Because the plaintiffs had not established title to the disputed land, no question of adverse possession against them arose.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession is a statutory method of acquiring title to land by limitation. It presupposes another person’s ownership and requires possession with an intention to hold the property in opposition to the world, together with the owner’s knowledge of that assertion. The Court also referred to Austin on Jurisprudence.

predicates.title_recovery_proceeding: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking title to or possession of land.
predicates.adverse_possession_asserted: An opposing party claimed to have acquired title through long possession adverse to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_lacks_title: The claimant failed to establish ownership of the land against which adverse possession was asserted.

issues.definition: In a title or possession proceeding, an adverse-possession claim against a claimant does not arise if that claimant has not established title to the land.
